claims.text: Optimized TLP diffusion bonding of Ti-6Al-4V will produce an interdiffused, homogeneous joint.
A TLP-bonded Ti-6Al-4V repair will avoid hot cracking.
A TLP-bonded Ti-6Al-4V repair will outperform traditional fusion-weld repairs under aggressive operating conditions.
The damaged Ti-6Al-4V component is unsuitable for conventional fusion welding because of hot-cracking risk.
A low-melting-point Ni-based braze interlayer can be used for TLP repair of Ti-6Al-4V.
Bonding below the Ti-6Al-4V substrate solidus can be performed at approximately 950°C.
Calibrating dwell time can achieve optimal interdiffusion in the proposed joint.
The repaired component can be tested and operated under cyclic loading and thermal exposure up to 600°C.
The engineered joint region will be homogenized and free from liquation and hot-crack-inducing microsegregation.
Optimizing the repair can minimize brittle intermetallic phases in the joint.
TLP bonding initiates a transient liquid phase at the repair interface.
Controlled interdiffusion between braze and substrate causes isothermal solidification of the transient liquid.
The TLP process creates a crack-resistant joint without completely melting the base material.
The TLP-repaired joint will have higher mechanical integrity and improved fatigue and creep resistance than a fusion-welded repair.
The TLP-repaired joint will have superior high-temperature stability relative to a fusion-welded repair.
Fusion welding involves melting and rapid solidification and can cause hot cracking.
Fusion-welded repairs have weakened mechanical performance under aggressive service conditions.
The repair's effectiveness depends on optimizing the Ni-based braze composition and dwell time to avoid brittle intermetallic formation.
Small deviations in interlayer composition or dwell time may cause brittle phase formation.
Long-term performance under combined cyclic thermal and mechanical loading remains unvalidated.
